paragraphs.title: The Uncertainty of Fate and the Preference for Life

easy.explanation: Ecclesiastes says there is one event to the righteous and to the wicked.
easy.q: What happens alike to the righteous and the wicked?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “For the living know that they shall die.”
The KJV says, “a living dog is better than a dead lion.”
easy.q: What is better than a dead lion?

answers: The living still have awareness and hope
The living can avoid every sorrow
medium.explanation: The living know, have hope, and still participate in what happens under the sun.
medium.q: Why does the passage present life as preferable to death?

answers: People control exactly when trouble comes
People cannot know their time, and death ends their earthly participation
medium.explanation: The passage emphasizes that people cannot know their time, and the dead have no further portion in what is done under the sun.
medium.q: How does the passage connect uncertainty with death?

medium.explanation: “Portion” means a share or participation in what is happening.
medium.q: In the phrase “they have any more a portion,” what does “portion” mean?

answers: A person cannot determine his earthly fate simply from his moral standing
There is no difference between good and evil
challenge.explanation: The passage stresses that similar events may come to people with very different character.
challenge.q: What conclusion follows from the fact that one event comes to both the righteous and the wicked?

answers: Life allows awareness and participation, even when one lacks status
challenge.explanation: The contrast shows that life itself is better than impressive status that is no longer active.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between a living dog and a dead lion emphasize?

answers: Love, hatred, envy, and any further portion in earthly affairs
challenge.explanation: The KJV says their love, hatred, and envy have perished, and they have no more a portion in anything done under the sun.
challenge.q: What is said to have perished after death?

short_answers.question: What does the KJV say is in the hand of God?
short_answers.answer: The righteous, the wise, and their works.
short_answers.explanation: Ecclesiastes 9:1 says that the righteous, the wise, and their works are in God’s hand.

short_answers.question: What has been forgotten concerning the dead?
short_answers.explanation: The passage says, “the memory of them is forgotten.”

short_answers.question: What is no longer found in the dead according to verse 5?
short_answers.answer: Knowledge of anything and any further reward.
short_answers.explanation: The dead know not any thing and have no more a reward.

paragraphs.title: Joy in Life and Action in the Present

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy.”
easy.q: What does Ecclesiastes tell the reader to eat?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “drink thy wine with a merry heart.”
easy.q: What should a person drink with a merry heart?

easy.explanation: Ecclesiastes says, “Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest.”
easy.q: With whom should a person live joyfully?

answers: There is no work, device, knowledge, or wisdom in the grave
People know exactly when they will die
medium.explanation: The passage says there is no work, device, knowledge, or wisdom in the grave.
medium.q: Why does Ecclesiastes urge people to act now?

answers: Both are ways of using one’s portion during life
medium.explanation: The passage presents food, companionship, and diligent work as part of a person’s portion in life.
medium.q: How are enjoyment and work connected in this passage?

medium.explanation: “Labour” refers to the work and effort a person undertakes.
medium.q: In the phrase “the labour which thou takest,” what does “labour” mean?

answers: Act diligently with the opportunities and abilities available now
Avoid effort because life is temporary
challenge.explanation: The command calls for vigorous action while a person is alive and able to work.
challenge.q: What practical principle is expressed by “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might”?

answers: They are presented as gifts and responsibilities belonging to earthly life
They belong only to the dead
challenge.explanation: Joyful married life is described as part of a person’s portion in this life and in his labour.
challenge.q: What relationship is shown between love, marriage, and one’s “portion”?

answers: It also commands purposeful and diligent work
It promises that life will last forever
It guarantees that everyone will become wealthy
challenge.explanation: The passage combines enjoyment of life with a command to do one’s work with strength.
challenge.q: What keeps the passage from making pleasure its only message?

short_answers.question: What does God now accept according to verse 7?
short_answers.explanation: The verse says, “for God now accepteth thy works.”

short_answers.question: What should always be white?
short_answers.explanation: The command is, “Let thy garments be always white.”

short_answers.question: What should the reader’s hand do?
short_answers.answer: Whatever it finds to do, with might.
short_answers.explanation: The KJV commands, “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.”

paragraphs.title: No Guarantee of Success Through Talent

easy.explanation: Ecclesiastes says that the race is not always to the swift.
easy.q: Does the race always go to the swift?

easy.explanation: The verse says riches do not necessarily come to men of understanding.
People are compared to fish taken in a net and birds caught in a snare.
easy.q: What animals illustrate people being caught suddenly?

answers: Personal advantages do not guarantee success
Strength is more important than timing
medium.explanation: The passage lists several abilities but says that success does not automatically follow them.
medium.q: What does the list of the swift, strong, wise, and skilled teach?

answers: Time and chance may happen to everyone
medium.explanation: The KJV says, “time and chance happeneth to them all.”
medium.q: Why may a person fail despite having great abilities?

medium.explanation: A snare is a trap used to catch birds.
medium.q: What is a “snare” in the phrase “the birds that are caught in the snare”?

answers: Talent may help, but it does not ensure the outcome
Talent has no relation to action
challenge.explanation: The swift, strong, wise, and skilled may still be affected by time and chance.
challenge.q: What is the difference between talent and guaranteed success in this passage?

answers: Danger can arrive suddenly and without warning
People always know when trouble will come
challenge.explanation: The image shows that people may be caught suddenly in an evil time.
challenge.q: What idea is reinforced by the image of fish and birds being caught?

answers: People do not know their time
challenge.explanation: Because a person does not know his time, he cannot rely completely on his abilities to secure the outcome.
challenge.q: How does verse 12 explain why talent cannot guarantee success?

short_answers.question: What happens to the swift, strong, wise, and skilled?
short_answers.answer: They are not guaranteed the expected results.
short_answers.explanation: The race, battle, bread, riches, and favour do not necessarily go to those with the corresponding abilities.

short_answers.question: What happens to the sons of men in an evil time?
short_answers.explanation: The verse says they are snared in an evil time when it falls suddenly upon them.

short_answers.question: What two things happen to everyone?
short_answers.explanation: Ecclesiastes says, “time and chance happeneth to them all.”

paragraphs.title: The Power of Wisdom and the Limits of Recognition

easy.explanation: The passage says that a poor wise man delivered the city by his wisdom.

answers: A great king who besieged it
easy.explanation: A great king came against the city, besieged it, and built bulwarks against it.
The final verse says, “Wisdom is better than weapons of war.”
easy.q: What is better than weapons of war?

answers: A poor wise man saves the city but is forgotten
A weak king saves the city and is remembered
A large city defeats a wise man
medium.explanation: The poor wise man delivers the city, yet no one remembers him afterward.
medium.q: What is the central contrast in the story of the city?

answers: They express wisdom rather than mere authority or force
They are always heard by everyone
medium.explanation: The passage values calm, wise speech over the loud command of a ruler among fools.
medium.q: Why may the words of wise men in quiet be better than the cry of a ruler?

medium.explanation: The man is described as poor in possessions, though he is wise enough to save the city.
medium.q: In the phrase “a poor wise man,” what does “poor” mean?

answers: Wisdom can be useful even when it receives no public honor
Only wealthy people can be wise
challenge.explanation: The man’s wisdom saves the city even though no one remembers him.
challenge.q: What does the poor man’s being forgotten teach about wisdom and recognition?

answers: One person’s wrongdoing can damage a great benefit
challenge.explanation: The statement acknowledges that wisdom is valuable, yet one sinner can still destroy much good.
challenge.q: How does “one sinner destroyeth much good” qualify the praise of wisdom?

answers: Wisdom is stronger than force, but it does not guarantee honor or protection from all harm
Wisdom has no value beside power
Wisdom guarantees that a person will be remembered forever
challenge.explanation: Wisdom can deliver a city and surpass weapons, but the wise may be despised or forgotten, and one sinner may destroy much good.
challenge.q: What balanced conclusion about wisdom emerges from the passage?

short_answers.question: What did the poor wise man use to deliver the city?
short_answers.explanation: The text says, “he by his wisdom delivered the city.”

short_answers.question: What happened to the poor wise man afterward?
short_answers.explanation: Although he saved the city, no one remembered that poor man.

short_answers.question: What can one sinner destroy?
short_answers.explanation: The final verse states, “one sinner destroyeth much good.”
